original.description: A line of Belgian infantry lying prone along the verge of a dirt road, firing to the left towards a hedgerow, packs still on their backs. They wear the dark blue greatcoat and the oilcloth-covered shako of the pre-1915 Belgian army, and carry Mauser rifles; a road curves away empty to the right.
original.photographer: not established — an agency photograph as reprinted in the illustrated press
original.archive: Published in Le Miroir, no. 38, p. 11, under the caption 'La Belgique envahie a gardé son sang-froid', and in the Russian periodical 'Velikaya voyna v obrazakh i kartinakh' (The Great War in Images and Pictures), ed. Ivan Lazarevsky, publisher D. Ya. Makovsky, 1914; the Commons record credits Aleksandr Matveyevich Azancheev (1870–1937) as the author of that Russian publication. Digitised from the Russian State Library and Tomsk library copies.
original.licence: public domain — published in the Russian Empire before 7 November 1917, and in the United States before 1 January 1931

caption: Belgian infantry in the fighting line in the suburbs of Herstal, north-east of Liège, August 1914 — the dark blue greatcoat and oilcloth shako the army still wore in 1914. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
credit: Original photograph: photographer not established; published in Le Miroir no. 38 (1914) and in 'The Great War in Images and Pictures' (Moscow, 1914); public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
notes: Supplied by Dave 2026-08-23. CAUTION for the image review (sand-y0u.7): the caption is the illustrated press's, not an archive record. Le Miroir and its Russian counterpart printed a great deal of posed and re-captioned material in 1914, and a firing line strung along an open road verge in full view, with packs still on, reads more like a demonstration or a manoeuvre than a fight. The uniforms and the rifles are right for the Belgian army in August 1914 and the place may well be Herstal; whether this is the defence of Liège or a photograph captioned as it is not established. The pack's caption therefore says where and when the publication places it and claims nothing about the moment.
